lessons.title: VLOOKUP, exact match
learn: Why VLOOKUP breaks when columns move
lessons.mac:
⌘ + T (or fn + F4) toggles $ signs while you edit a formula
⌘ + D fills down
⌘ + Z undoes
On the web the same jobs use F4, Ctrl + D and Ctrl + Z

steps.say: Here's the order sheet we'll finish in this lesson. Every order picks up its rate from the product master on the right, so nobody types a price by hand and nobody types a wrong one.
In this lesson you'll learn three things.

acts.t:
In this lesson
1. VLOOKUP with an exact match
2. Locking the lookup table with $ signs
3. Why VLOOKUP breaks when columns move

Practice sheet: S07-01

steps.say: VLOOKUP takes four arguments. What to look for, the table to search, which column to bring back, and whether you want an exact match. The code you look for must sit in the first column of the table.

acts.t:
VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, col_index_num, [range_lookup])

lookup_value: what you are looking for (the product code)
table_array: the table to search; the code must be in its first column
col_index_num: which column of that table to return, counting from 1
range_lookup: FALSE for an exact match

steps.say: Here's the practice sheet. Orders are in columns A to E, and the product master is in columns H to L. Column D needs the rate for each product code.
In cell D2, type equals VLOOKUP, open bracket.
The first argument is the value to look up. Type B2, the product code of this order, and a comma.
Next comes the table. Type H2 colon L11, then press Command T to lock it with dollar signs, so the range stays put when we copy the formula down. Then a comma.
Rate is the fourth column of this table. Code is one, Product two, Category three, Rate four. Type 4 and a comma.
Last, type FALSE, which means exact match only. Close the bracket and press Return. Basmati Rice comes back at six hundred and forty rupees.
Select D2 to D13 and press Command D to fill down. Every rate fills in, and the Amount column calculates on its own.

acts.h: Select D2:D13 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Look at the last order. Code P111 isn't in the master, so VLOOKUP shows hash N A, which means not available. That's a data problem to fix in the master, not a formula problem.
Now the classic VLOOKUP trap. Say a colleague inserts a new column inside the master. Click J1, then on the Home tab choose Insert, Insert Sheet Columns.
The Rate column now shows category names, and Amount shows hash VALUE. The formula still asks for column four, but Rate has moved to column five. VLOOKUP counts columns. It doesn't follow them.
Press Command Z to undo the insert. In lesson S07-04 you'll meet XLOOKUP, which doesn't break this way.
Lookups stay live. Change the code in B2 to P107 and press Return. The rate switches to two thousand three hundred and fifty rupees. Then put P103 back.
A quick word on Mac keys.

acts.t:
Mac corner
⌘ + T (or fn + F4) toggles $ signs while you edit a formula
⌘ + D fills down
⌘ + Z undoes
On the web the same jobs use F4, Ctrl + D and Ctrl + Z

steps.say: Here's the recap.

acts.t:
Recap
• VLOOKUP(code, table, column number, FALSE) finds an exact match
• Lock the table with ⌘ + T before you copy the formula down
• Insert a column inside the table and the column number points to the wrong data

steps.say: Your turn. In column F, bring back the GST percentage for each order with VLOOKUP. GST is the fifth column of the master. The answer is on the S07-01 Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge
In F2:F13, return the GST % for each order with VLOOKUP.
Hint: GST % is column 5 of $H$2:$L$11.
Answer: sheet S07-01 Done, column F

lessons.title: Approximate match: commission and discount slabs
learn: Sorted bands with VLOOKUP and XLOOKUP

steps.say: This sheet works out every salesperson's commission rate from a slab table. Sales of five lakh or more earn four percent, ten lakh or more earn five percent, and so on. One formula handles every band.
Here's what you'll learn.

acts.t:
In this lesson
1. Approximate match with VLOOKUP (TRUE)
2. The same slab lookup with XLOOKUP
3. The mistakes that give wrong slab rates

Practice sheet: S07-02

steps.say: With approximate match, Excel finds the largest value that is less than or equal to the sales figure. For that to work, the slab table must start at zero and be sorted from smallest to largest.

acts.t:
Slab lookups
VLOOKUP(sales, slab_table, 2, TRUE)
TRUE = approximate match: the largest 'Sales From' value that is ≤ the sales

XLOOKUP(sales, from_column, rate_column, , -1)
match_mode -1 = exact match, or the next smaller item

The slab table must start at 0 and be sorted smallest to largest

steps.say: Here's the practice sheet. Sales are in column B and the slab table is in H1 to J6. Each Sales From value is the lower edge of a band.
Click C2 and type equals VLOOKUP, open bracket, B2, comma.
Now the slab table. Type H2 colon I6, press Command T to lock it, and type a comma.
We want the rate, the second column of the slab table. Type 2, a comma, then TRUE for approximate match. Close the bracket and press Return.
Aarav sold one lakh eighty-five thousand. That's below two lakh, so he lands in the first band at two percent. Fill the formula down with Command D.

acts.h: Select C2:C13 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Check Vikram in row six. His sales are exactly two lakh, so he gets three percent. Approximate match includes the lower edge of each band.
Now the XLOOKUP version in column E. Type equals XLOOKUP, open bracket, B2, comma, then the Sales From column H2 to H6, locked with Command T, and a comma.
The return column is I2 to I6, locked. Then two commas, because we skip the not-found argument. Then minus one, which means exact match or the next smaller item. Close the bracket and press Return.
Fill it down with Command D. The two columns agree. XLOOKUP doesn't need a column number, so it keeps working if someone rearranges the slab table.

acts.h: Select E2:E13 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Here's a typical mistake. Suppose the first slab starts at fifty thousand instead of zero. Click H2, type 50000 and press Return.
Neha's sales of forty-five thousand are now below the first band, so both lookups return hash N A. The slab table must always start at zero. Press Command Z to put the zero back.
The other trap is an unsorted slab table. Approximate match assumes ascending order, so a shuffled table gives wrong rates with no error at all. Always sort the slabs smallest to largest.

acts.t:
Avoid wrong slab rates
• Start the table at 0
• Sort 'Sales From' smallest to largest
• Use TRUE in VLOOKUP, or -1 in XLOOKUP
• Omitting the 4th VLOOKUP argument also means TRUE, so always type it

steps.say: Prove it's live. Change Aarav's sales in B2 to 2,10,000. He moves up to the three percent band straight away.
Here's the recap.

acts.t:
Recap
• Approximate match returns the band an amount falls into
• VLOOKUP(…, TRUE) or XLOOKUP(…, , -1) both work
• The slab table must start at 0 and be sorted ascending

steps.say: Your turn. In column F, return the slab name, such as Gold or Platinum, using XLOOKUP and column J of the slab table. The answer is on the S07-02 Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge
In F2:F13, return the slab name (Bronze to Diamond) with XLOOKUP.
Hint: return $J$2:$J$6 with match_mode -1.
Answer: sheet S07-02 Done, column F

lessons.title: HLOOKUP, INDEX and MATCH
lessons.mac:
Nothing changes on a Mac for these functions.
Tip: click fx next to the formula bar (or press Shift + F3) to open the
Formula Builder, which names every argument as you fill it in.

steps.say: This little report answers two questions. What did all regions sell in a chosen month, and what did one region sell in that month? Change the month or region in yellow and every answer updates.
Here's the plan.

acts.t:
In this lesson
1. HLOOKUP: look across a row of headings
2. MATCH: find a position
3. INDEX + MATCH: a two-way lookup by month and region

Practice sheet: S07-03

steps.say: Three functions today. HLOOKUP is VLOOKUP turned sideways. MATCH tells you where something sits in a list. INDEX returns the value at a row and column position.

acts.t:
HLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, row_index_num, [range_lookup])
Searches the top row, returns from the row number you give

MATCH(lookup_value, lookup_array, [match_type])
Returns the position; use 0 for an exact match

INDEX(array, row_num, [column_num])
Returns the value at that row and column of the array

steps.say: Here's the practice sheet. Months run across row one, regions run down column A, and the inputs are in J2 and J3.
First, the month total with HLOOKUP. In J5, type equals HLOOKUP, open bracket, J2 for the month, and a comma.
The table is A1 to G7, including the Total row. Totals are in the seventh row of that table, so type 7. Then FALSE for exact match, close the bracket and press Return.

That's the July total for all five regions. Now MATCH. In J6, type equals MATCH, open bracket, J3 for the region, comma, A2 to A6, comma, zero for exact match. Close and press Return. West is the fourth region.
Do the same for the month. In J7, type equals MATCH, open bracket, J2, comma, B1 to G1, comma, zero. July is the fourth month in the list.
Now INDEX. In J8, type equals INDEX, open bracket, then B2 to G6, the numbers only, and a comma.
The row number is in J6 and the column number is in J7. Type J6, comma, J7, close the bracket and press Return. That's West in July.
Most people put the two MATCH formulas straight inside INDEX. Click J8 and type the one-cell version, with MATCH for the row and MATCH for the column. Same answer, no helper cells.
A common mistake is text that doesn't match exactly. Type July in J2 instead of Jul. Every lookup returns hash N A, because the heading says Jul.
Fix it by typing Jul. To stop this for good, a dropdown list on J2 is the answer, which you'll build in section S08.
Now change the month to Sep. The month total and West's figure both update.
A Mac note.

acts.t:
Mac corner
Nothing changes on a Mac for these functions.
Tip: click fx next to the formula bar (or press Shift + F3) to open the
Formula Builder, which names every argument as you fill it in.

steps.say: Here's the recap.

acts.t:
Recap
• HLOOKUP searches the top row and returns from a row number
• MATCH(value, list, 0) gives a position
• INDEX(numbers, MATCH(row), MATCH(column)) is a two-way lookup that survives inserted columns

steps.say: Your turn. In J10, return the region's total from April to September. Hint: use zero as the column number inside INDEX to get the whole row, then wrap it in SUM. The answer is on the Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge
In J10, total April to September for the region in J3.
Hint: =SUM(INDEX(B2:G6, MATCH(…), 0))
Answer: sheet S07-03 Done, cell J10

lessons.title: XLOOKUP: the modern lookup
learn: Exact match, not-found text, look left
lessons.mac:
XLOOKUP needs Microsoft 365, Excel 2021 or later.
On Excel 2019 or older for Mac it shows #NAME?.
Check yours: Excel menu > About Excel.

steps.say: Type an employee ID in the yellow cell and this panel returns the name, salary, and name, department and location together. All of it uses XLOOKUP, and the ID column sits to the right of the name, which VLOOKUP can't handle.
Here's what's coming.

acts.t:
In this lesson
1. XLOOKUP with an exact match
2. A friendly 'Not found' message
3. Looking to the left, and returning several columns at once

Practice sheet: S07-04

steps.say: XLOOKUP needs only three arguments. What to find, where to find it, and what to bring back. Exact match is the default, so there's no FALSE to remember.

acts.t:
XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array, [if_not_found], [match_mode], [search_mode])

lookup_value: what you are looking for
lookup_array: the single column to search
return_array: the column (or columns) to bring back
if_not_found: text to show when nothing matches
match_mode: 0 exact (default), -1 next smaller, 1 next larger, 2 wildcard

steps.say: Here's the practice sheet. Fifteen employees, with Emp ID in column D. The ID to find is in H1.
In H2, type equals XLOOKUP, open bracket, then H1, the ID we're looking for, and a comma.
The lookup array is the Emp ID column, D2 to D16, and a comma.
The return array is the name column, A2 to A16. It's to the left of the IDs, and XLOOKUP doesn't mind. Add a comma.
For if not found, type Not found in double quotes. Close the bracket and press Return. Employee 1007 is Nikhil Rao.

acts.h: Type "Not found") and press Return

steps.say: Now the salary. In H3, type equals XLOOKUP, open bracket, H1, comma, D2 to D16, comma, E2 to E15, close the bracket and press Return.
Hash VALUE. The lookup array has fifteen rows but the return array has only fourteen. Both ranges must be the same size. Retype it with E2 to E16.
One lakh eighteen thousand rupees. Now several columns at once. In H5, type the same start, H1, comma, D2 to D16, comma, but return A2 to C16, three columns.
Press Return. Name, department and location spill across H5 to J5 from one formula.
Now test it. Change H1 to EMP1099, an ID that doesn't exist. H2 says Not found, as we asked. H3 shows hash N A because we didn't give it a message.
Put EMP1007 back in H1 and everything returns.
A Mac note.

acts.t:
Mac corner
XLOOKUP needs Microsoft 365, Excel 2021 or later.
On Excel 2019 or older for Mac it shows #NAME?.
Check yours: Excel menu > About Excel.

steps.say: Here's the recap.

acts.t:
Recap
• XLOOKUP(value, search column, return column) is exact by default
• It looks left or right and never breaks when columns are inserted
• Return several columns at once, and set your own 'Not found' text

steps.say: Your turn. G8 holds the name Kavya Iyer. In H8, return her Emp ID with XLOOKUP. This time you search the name column and return the ID column. The answer is on the Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge
In H8, return the Emp ID for the name in G8.
Hint: search A2:A16, return D2:D16, show "Not found" if missing.
Answer: sheet S07-04 Done, cell H8

lessons.title: XLOOKUP advanced
lessons.mac:
All of this works the same on Mac, Microsoft 365.
To see what (B2:B16=H1)*(D2:D16=H2) returns, select that part
in the formula bar and press fn + F9, then ⌘ + Z to undo.

steps.say: This panel answers four everyday questions from a sales register. What did Rohan sell in ceiling fans, when was his last sale, what's the first cooker sale, and where does his last sale sit in the list.
Here's what you'll learn.

acts.t:
In this lesson
1. XLOOKUP with two conditions
2. Find the last match instead of the first
3. Wildcards, and XMATCH for positions

Practice sheet: S07-05

steps.say: Two arguments do the heavy lifting today. Match mode two turns on wildcards. Search mode minus one searches from the bottom up, which gives you the last match.

acts.t:
XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array, [if_not_found], [match_mode], [search_mode])

match_mode 2: wildcards  * any text, ? one character
search_mode -1: search last to first

XMATCH(lookup_value, lookup_array, [match_mode], [search_mode])
Same options, returns a position

steps.say: Here's the practice sheet. The register is sorted by date, and the questions are in column G.
Two conditions first. In H3, type equals XLOOKUP, open bracket, 1, comma. We look for the number one, and you'll see why in a moment.

Now the lookup array. Open a bracket, B2 to B16 equals H1, close it, then star, then open a bracket, D2 to D16 equals H2, close it, and a comma. Each test gives TRUE or FALSE, and multiplying them gives one only where both are true.
Return E2 to E16, type No sale in quotes, close the bracket and press Return. Rohan's ceiling fan sale was twenty-eight thousand nine hundred rupees.

acts.h: Type E2:E16,"No sale") and press Return

steps.say: Next, his last sale. In H4, type equals XLOOKUP, open bracket, H1, comma, B2 to B16, comma, A2 to A16 for the date, comma, None in quotes, comma.
Match mode zero for exact, comma, then search mode minus one to search from the bottom. Close the bracket and press Return. His last sale was on the twenty-first of May.

Now wildcards. H5 holds star Cooker star, meaning any text containing Cooker. In H6, type equals XLOOKUP, open bracket, H5, comma, D2 to D16, comma, E2 to E16, comma, No match in quotes. Close and press Return.
It says No match, even though there are cooker sales. Without match mode two, the stars are treated as ordinary characters. Retype it with comma 2 at the end.
Twenty-three thousand five hundred, the first pressure cooker sale. Finally XMATCH. In H7, type equals XMATCH, open bracket, H1, comma, B2 to B16, comma, 0, comma, minus 1. Close and press Return.
Twelve. Rohan's last sale is the twelfth row of the list. XMATCH is the modern MATCH, and it pairs well with INDEX.
Change the salesperson in H1 to Priya Nair. Her last sale date and position update. Her ceiling fan amount changes too.

acts.h: Type Priya Nair and press Return

steps.say: A Mac note.

acts.t:
Mac corner
All of this works the same on Mac, Microsoft 365.
To see what (B2:B16=H1)*(D2:D16=H2) returns, select that part
in the formula bar and press fn + F9, then ⌘ + Z to undo.

steps.say: Here's the recap.

acts.t:
Recap
• Several conditions: XLOOKUP(1, (test1)*(test2), return)
• Last match: search_mode -1
• Wildcards need match_mode 2; XMATCH returns positions

steps.say: Your turn. In H9, find the amount of the last sale of the product in H2. The answer is on the S07-05 Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge
In H9, return the amount of the LAST sale of the product in H2.
Hint: search D2:D16, return E2:E16, search_mode -1.
Answer: sheet S07-05 Done, cell H9

lessons.title: CHOOSE, CHOOSECOLS and CHOOSEROWS
lessons.mac:
CHOOSECOLS and CHOOSEROWS need Microsoft 365 (Mac, Windows or web).
In Excel 2021 for Mac they show #NAME?.

steps.say: Pick scenario one, two or three in B1, and the growth rate and next year's revenue follow. Below it, the branch table is reshaped by formula, with columns reordered and rows picked out, without copying anything.
Here's the plan.

acts.t:
In this lesson
1. CHOOSE: pick a value by its number
2. CHOOSECOLS: pick and reorder columns
3. CHOOSEROWS: pick rows, counting from the top or bottom

Practice sheet: S07-06

steps.say: CHOOSE takes a number and a list, and returns the item at that position. CHOOSECOLS and CHOOSEROWS do the same with the columns or rows of a range. A negative number counts from the end.

acts.t:
CHOOSE(index_num, value1, [value2], …)
CHOOSECOLS(array, col_num1, [col_num2], …)
CHOOSEROWS(array, row_num1, [row_num2], …)

index_num / col_num / row_num: position, starting at 1
Negative numbers count from the end: -1 is the last

steps.say: Here's the practice sheet. The scenario number is in B1, and the branch table is in A8 to E14.
In B2, type equals CHOOSE, open bracket, B1, comma. Then the three names in quotes, separated by commas: Conservative, Base, Optimistic. Close the bracket and press Return.
B1 is two, so we get Base. In B3, type equals CHOOSE, open bracket, B1, comma, 8 percent, comma, 12 percent, comma, 15 percent. Close and press Return.
Twelve percent growth, and B5 already shows next year's revenue of one crore thirty-four lakh forty thousand rupees. Change B1 to 3 and watch both cells switch to the optimistic case.
Here's the common mistake. Type 4 in B1. There's no fourth item, so CHOOSE returns hash VALUE, and every cell that depends on it does too.
Keep B1 between one and the number of items. A dropdown list from section S08 stops this. Type 2 to go back to Base.
Now CHOOSECOLS. In G8, type equals CHOOSECOLS, open bracket, A8 to E14, the whole table with headings, and a comma.
We want City first, then Branch, then Q2 Sales. That's columns 3, 1 and 5. Type them, close the bracket and press Return. The new table spills, in our order.
Now CHOOSEROWS. In A17, type equals CHOOSEROWS, open bracket, A8 to E14, comma, 1 for the heading row, comma, minus 1 for the last row. Close and press Return.
The heading and the last branch, Hinjewadi. If you add a branch to the table and extend the range, minus one always picks the newest row.
A Mac note.

acts.t:
Mac corner
CHOOSECOLS and CHOOSEROWS need Microsoft 365 (Mac, Windows or web).
In Excel 2021 for Mac they show #NAME?.

steps.say: Here's the recap.

acts.t:
Recap
• CHOOSE(n, a, b, c) picks the nth item: handy for scenarios
• CHOOSECOLS reorders or drops columns without copying
• CHOOSEROWS picks rows; -1 is the last row

steps.say: Your turn. In G17, use CHOOSECOLS to show Q2 Sales first and City second. The answer is on the S07-06 Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge
In G17, show Q2 Sales then City for every branch, with headings.
Hint: =CHOOSECOLS(A8:E14, 5, 3)
Answer: sheet S07-06 Done, cell G17

lessons.title: INDIRECT, OFFSET, ADDRESS, ROW and COLUMN
learn: Pull data from a sheet named in a cell

steps.say: Type a branch name in B1 and B2 totals that branch's own sheet. On the right, a rolling total always covers the latest three months, so next month you just type the new figure.
Here's what you'll learn.

acts.t:
In this lesson
1. INDIRECT: build a reference from text, such as a sheet name in a cell
2. OFFSET: a range that moves, for rolling totals
3. ADDRESS, ROW and COLUMN

Practice sheet: S07-07, plus sheets Mumbai, Delhi and Bengaluru

steps.say: INDIRECT turns text into a live reference. OFFSET starts at a cell, moves down and across, and returns a range of the size you ask for.

acts.t:
INDIRECT(ref_text, [a1])
ref_text: a reference written as text, e.g. "Mumbai!B2:B13"

OFFSET(reference, rows, cols, [height], [width])
Start at reference, move rows down and cols across,
then return a range height × width

ADDRESS(row_num, column_num) returns an address as text, e.g. $E$7

steps.say: First, look at the Mumbai sheet. Months are in A2 to A13 and sales in B2 to B13. Delhi and Bengaluru have the same layout.
Back on S07-07, click B2. Type equals SUM, open bracket, INDIRECT, open bracket, B1, then an ampersand to join on the text exclamation mark B2 colon B13 in quotes.
Close both brackets and press Return. That's the Mumbai total, read from the Mumbai sheet.
Now type Delhi in B1. The total jumps to the Delhi sheet. One formula, any branch.
Here's the common mistake. Type Chennai, a branch with no sheet. INDIRECT can't find it, so you get hash REF. The text must match a real sheet name. Type Delhi again.

If a sheet name has spaces, wrap it in single quotes inside the text, like quote, apostrophe, Navi Mumbai, apostrophe, exclamation mark. Now the rolling total. In H1, type equals COUNT, open bracket, E2 to E13. Six months have data so far.
In H2, type equals SUM, open bracket, OFFSET, open bracket, E1, comma. E1 is our starting point, the heading.
Move down H1 minus 2 rows, which lands on July. Comma, zero columns across, comma, a height of 3 rows, comma, width 1. Close both brackets and press Return.
That's July, August and September. Now type October's figure in E8, fourteen lakh seventy-five thousand. The count becomes seven and the total rolls forward to August to October.
Last, ADDRESS with ROW and COLUMN. In H3, type equals ADDRESS, open bracket, H1 plus ROW of E1, comma, COLUMN of E1. Close and press Return. It tells us the latest figure sits in E8.
A note on speed.

acts.t:
Pro tip
INDIRECT and OFFSET are volatile: they recalculate after every change.
A few are fine. Thousands slow a workbook down.
INDEX(…):INDEX(…) does the same rolling range without being volatile.

steps.say: Here's the recap.

acts.t:
Recap
• INDIRECT(B1&"!B2:B13") reads the sheet named in B1
• OFFSET(start, down, across, height, width) gives a moving range
• ADDRESS, ROW and COLUMN turn positions into addresses and back

steps.say: Your turn. In H5, total the last three months again, but with INDEX instead of OFFSET. The answer is on the S07-07 Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge
In H5, total the last 3 months without OFFSET.
Hint: =SUM(INDEX(E2:E13,H1-2):INDEX(E2:E13,H1))
Answer: sheet S07-07 Done, cell H5

lessons.title: HYPERLINK and a contents sheet
learn: Links to cells, files and websites
lessons.mac:
⌘ + K opens Insert Link if you prefer a dialog.
To select a link cell without opening it, click and hold until the pointer changes,
or use the arrow keys.

steps.say: This is a contents sheet for the whole workbook. Each blue link jumps to a sheet, one opens the GST portal, and one lands on a single cell. In a twenty-sheet MIS file, a page like this saves your team a lot of scrolling.
Here's the plan.

acts.t:
In this lesson
1. HYPERLINK to sheets, built from a list of names
2. Links to a single cell and to a website
3. Why sheet names need single quotes

Practice sheet: S07-08

steps.say: HYPERLINK takes a destination and the text to show. For a place inside this workbook, start the destination with a hash sign.

acts.t:
HYPERLINK(link_location, [friendly_name])

link_location: where to go
  "#'S07-01'!A1"  a cell in this workbook (note the #)
  "https://www.gst.gov.in"  a website
friendly_name: the text shown in the cell

Sheet names with spaces or hyphens need single quotes

steps.say: Here's the practice sheet. Sheet names are in column A, and the links go in column B.
In B2, type equals HYPERLINK, open bracket. Then in double quotes, a hash sign and a single quote. Close the quotes, and add an ampersand.
Now A2, the sheet name, another ampersand, and in double quotes: single quote, exclamation mark, A1. Close the quotes and type a comma.
For the friendly name, type Go to, with a space, in quotes, then an ampersand and A2. Close the bracket and press Return.

acts.h: Type "Go to "&A2) and press Return

steps.say: Fill it down to B8 with Command D. Every sheet now has its own link.

acts.h: Select B2:B8 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Click Go to S07-04. Excel jumps straight to that sheet. Come back to S07-08.

Here's the mistake people make. If you leave out the single quotes, the destination becomes hash S07-04 exclamation A1. Because the name has a hyphen, Excel can't read it and says the reference isn't valid. Keep the quotes, and the same formula works for names with spaces too.

acts.t:
Common mistake
=HYPERLINK("#"&A2&"!A1", …)  fails for S07-04 or 'Sales Report'
=HYPERLINK("#'"&A2&"'!A1", …)  always works

steps.say: A link to a website. In B10, type equals HYPERLINK, open bracket, the address https colon slash slash www dot gst dot gov dot in in quotes, comma, Open GST portal in quotes. Close and press Return.

acts.h: Type =HYPERLINK("https://www.gst.gov.in","Open GST portal") and press Return

steps.say: And a link to one cell. In B11, type equals HYPERLINK, open bracket, then hash, quote S07-07 quote, exclamation mark, H2, all in double quotes. Comma, Rolling total in quotes. Close and press Return.
A Mac note.

acts.t:
Mac corner
⌘ + K opens Insert Link if you prefer a dialog.
To select a link cell without opening it, click and hold until the pointer changes,
or use the arrow keys.

lessons.title: Challenge 5: build an invoice lookup
learn: Product, rate and GST rate by code

steps.say: Challenge time. This is a GST tax invoice for a customer in Pune. The codes and quantities are filled in. Your job is to complete everything in yellow using lookups.
Here are your tasks. They're also written on the sheet from column J onwards.

acts.t:
Challenge 5
1. In C6, one XLOOKUP returns Product, Rate and GST % from 'Product Master'
2. Show "Check code" when a code is missing
3. Copy C6 down to C11
4. F: Taxable = Qty × Rate   5. G: GST = Taxable × GST %   6. H: Line Total
7. Row 13: totals

Check: H6 = ₹2,688

steps.say: Pause the video now and try it. When you're ready, play it again and we'll solve it together.

acts.t:
Pause the video and try it now.
Practice sheet: S07-09
Product list: sheet 'Product Master'

steps.say: Here's the solution. First, glance at the Product Master sheet. Code is in column A, and Product, Rate and GST are side by side in B to D.

acts.h: Go to the sheet Product Master

steps.say: Back on S07-09, click C6. Type equals XLOOKUP, open bracket, A6, comma. Then the codes on Product Master, A2 to A11, locked with dollar signs, and a comma.
For the return array, take all three columns, B2 to D11, also locked. Comma, then Check code in quotes. Close the bracket and press Return.

acts.h: Type 'Product Master'!$B$2:$D$11,"Check code") and press Return

steps.say: Product, rate and GST percent spill across C6 to E6 from one formula. Now select C6 to C11 and press Command D. Each row gets its own lookup.

acts.h: Select C6:C11 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Row ten shows Check code. P115 isn't in the master, so the rate stays empty. On a real invoice you'd fix the code before sending it.
Now the maths. In F6, type equals B6 times D6. Press Tab, and in G6 type equals F6 times E6. Press Tab, and in H6 type equals F6 plus G6, then Return.
Select F6 to H11 and press Command D to fill all three formulas down at once.

acts.h: Select F6:H11 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Finally the totals. In F13, type equals SUM of F6 to F11 and press Return. Then copy it across to G13 and H13 with Command R.

Check H6. Four bags of Basmati at six forty is two thousand five hundred and sixty, plus five percent GST, gives two thousand six hundred and eighty-eight rupees. Compare your sheet with S07-09 Answers.
Here's the recap of the section.

acts.t:
Section recap: Lookups
• VLOOKUP and HLOOKUP for older files; XLOOKUP for new work
• INDEX + MATCH for two-way lookups
• CHOOSE, INDIRECT, OFFSET and HYPERLINK for flexible models
• One XLOOKUP can return several columns
